title: True/False and Boolean Logic
learningObjectives: Define Boolean values as true or false.
Distinguish a Boolean literal from an expression that produces a Boolean result.
Trace simple Boolean conditions and predict their result.
Explain why Boolean results are used in decision-making.
Recognize boundary and language-specific truthiness mistakes.

understand.concept: Boolean logic represents two logical outcomes: true and false. Programs use them to represent whether a rule is satisfied, input passes a check, a loop should continue, or an action may proceed. Some languages have a dedicated Boolean type; others accept values in conditions through language-specific conversion rules. Learn the logical meaning without assuming every language behaves identically.
understand.whyItMatters: Boolean reasoning is the basis of program decisions, validation, filtering, tests and control flow. Developers must trace a condition and explain why it produces one outcome.
understand.analogy: A badge check can answer true if the badge is valid and false if it is not, then use that result to decide whether to unlock a door.
understand.analogyLimit: Real access systems may have extra states such as expired credentials or network failure. A Boolean model simplifies one decision and does not represent every possible failure.

explain.narrative:
Boolean values are the logical outcomes true and false. A condition is an expression that evaluates to one of these outcomes. The literal true is already a Boolean value; a condition such as score >= 50 computes a result from data. A variable can store that result using a descriptive name such as isOpen, hasStock, or meetsRequirement.

Languages differ: JavaScript uses true and false and also has truthy/falsy conversions; Python spells its Boolean literals True and False; C conditions follow its own scalar-expression rules. Learn the exact rules in each language course.

Read conditions as questions and trace the values. Boundary wording matters: “at least 18” includes 18, while “greater than 18” excludes it. Later topics cover comparisons in detail and combining conditions with AND, OR and NOT.

Common mistakes include reversing a condition, confusing the source data with the Boolean result, assuming non-Boolean values behave the same across languages, and writing complex rules before stating them plainly. A Boolean check also does not prove a real-world process succeeded; data may be incomplete or stale.

examples.title: Condition result
examples.explanation: stock > 0 evaluates to true, which is stored in hasStock.

examples.title: Boundary difference
examples.explanation: Greater-than excludes equality; greater-than-or-equal includes it.

examples.title: Trace a condition
examples.explanation: 250 >= 200 is true, so canBuy stores true.

examples.title: Check a requirement
examples.explanation: The condition evaluates a requirement and produces a Boolean result; password security must not depend on length alone.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Target completion
guidedTask.instructions: A learner completed 7 of 10 lessons. Store completed and requirement, evaluate completed >= requirement, save the result in isComplete, and print it. Then change completed to 10 and predict before running.
steps: Read the condition as a question.

independentTask.title: Independent: Shipping eligibility
independentTask.instructions: Create qualifiesForFreeShipping from orderTotal and freeShippingThreshold. It should be true when the total meets or exceeds the threshold. Test one value below, exactly equal, and above; record predictions before running.
requirements: Include the boundary in your condition.
Show three test cases and predicted outcomes.
Explain why the boundary test matters.

hints: Boolean outcomes are true or false.
A condition evaluates data to a logical result.
State the rule in plain language first.
Test below, at, and above the boundary.
Trace inputs manually when results surprise you.

questions.prompt: Which is a Boolean literal rather than a comparison expression?
questions.explanation: true is already a Boolean value; the comparisons compute Boolean results.

questions.prompt: If count equals 3, what is count > 3?

options: Price is less than or equal to budget
questions.answer: Price is less than or equal to budget
questions.explanation: The <= operator includes equality and checks that price does not exceed budget.

questions.prompt: Why do truthiness rules vary between languages?
options: Each language defines whether and how non-Boolean values work in conditions
questions.answer: Each language defines whether and how non-Boolean values work in conditions

questions.prompt: A passing score is 70 or higher. Which condition expresses that?
questions.explanation: The >= operator includes 70 and larger values.
